title: The Diagnostic Handbook (Sakikkû)

confidence.note: The date rests on a catalogue rubric, copied in the first millennium BCE, that credits the edition to Esagil-kin-apli under King Adad-apla-iddina (1068–1047 BCE); Geller calls him a scholar 'said to have lived' in the 11th century. The surviving tablets are later copies, and that he edited older omen collections rather than writing them is the scholarly consensus.

people: Esagil-kin-apli (fl. 11th century BCE), chief scholar (ummânu) credited with the edition
summary: A Babylonian scholar is credited with weaving centuries of medical omens into 40 tablets that read the body from head to foot; many entries link an illness to a god, demon or ghost.
body: Around 1060 BCE a Babylonian scholar named Esagil-kin-apli, chief scholar (*ummânu*) under King Adad-apla-iddina, is credited by a later catalogue note with a feat it calls unprecedented. The diagnostic omens of his day, the note says, were like twisted threads with no copy to consult. He wove them into a single edition of 40 tablets, arranged 'from cranium to feet', called *Sakikkû*, 'symptoms'.

Each entry runs on an if–then pattern: if the patient shows this sign, then this is the diagnosis or the outcome. Many entries add the 'hand' of a god, demon or ghost. Markham Geller reads that as an association with a deity rather than a cause; Nils Heeßel, whom he cites, takes it as the divine agent behind the illness. The opening tablets read omens met on the way to the bedside: a healer who passed a pig, a brick or a pregnant woman would probably find the patient would die. It predicted; treatment mostly lived in separate prescription texts.

How much of it was really his is doubtful. The credit comes from catalogue notes, and Geller treats him as a Babylonian counterpart to Hippocrates: one name that lent authority to a standardized body of texts, much as the Hippocratic name served for a corpus mostly written by anonymous authors.

links.note: The diagnostic omens belonged to the exorcist's art as well as the physician's.

title: The Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia

confidence.note: The tablets carry Ashurbanipal's library colophons, which fixes them to his reign. That the fragments form one twelve-part encyclopedia is a recent reconstruction based on a catalogue from Ashur; the original length (about 13,250 lines, of which some 43 percent survives) is an estimate.

people: Strahil Panayotov, Assyriologist who matched the Ashur catalogue to the Nineveh tablets
summary: Scribes of an Assyrian king compiled a medical encyclopedia of an estimated 13,000 lines, ordered from head to toe. Only recently did scholars realize the broken fragments were one work.
body: In the 7th century BCE, scribes working for the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled at Nineveh a vast handbook of remedies, now called the Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia. Its twelve treatises, about fifty large two-column tablets and an estimated 13,000 lines, start with the head, eyes, ears and teeth and work down to the feet. The broken tablets long looked like a random collection; only when a catalogue from the city of Ashur was reconstructed did scholars see they followed one plan. Since 2020 the NinMed project at the British Museum has been rebuilding and translating it.

links.note: Its editors worked in the same editorial tradition the later catalogues credit to Esagil-kin-apli.
The encyclopaedia is the physician's prescription literature at its fullest.

title: Imhotep, the physician who may not have been one

confidence.note: Two inscriptions from his lifetime place Imhotep at the court of Djoser in the 3rd Dynasty, though absolute dates for that dynasty carry decades of uncertainty. None of the early evidence connects him with medicine; the earliest surviving health-related reference is of the 4th century BCE, and scholars disagree about whether Manetho already linked him to medicine.

people: Imhotep (fl. 27th century BCE), official of King Djoser
William Osler (1849–1919), physician who in 1921 called him the first physician to emerge from antiquity
summary: Imhotep was a real royal official. The healer-god, and the 'first physician' of modern textbooks, came more than two thousand years later.
body: Imhotep was real. Two inscriptions from his own lifetime, one on the base of a statue of King Djoser, give his titles: royal seal-bearer, great of seers (a priest of Heliopolis) and overseer of sculptors. Those titles fit the tradition that he designed Djoser's Step Pyramid, Egypt's first monumental stone building, though no inscription says so, and one museum catalogue finds no evidence from Djoser's time. None calls him a physician.

His fame then grew for millennia. By the New Kingdom he was remembered as a sage and patron of scribes. In the Late Period he was worshipped near Memphis as a son of the god Ptah, and hundreds of bronze figurines show him seated with a papyrus on his lap. The earliest surviving health-related reference dates to the 4th century BCE, after which Greeks equated him with Asklepios.

William Osler, in lectures published in 1921, called him the first physician to stand out from the mists of antiquity. Part of that reputation may rest on an insertion. A fragment of Manetho credits a Third Dynasty king with medical skill that made Egyptians count him an Asklepios; a widely used English translation printed Imhotep's name into it. Patric Blomstedt and a newer translator reject that emendation, while Marina Escolano-Poveda reads Manetho as describing Imhotep as devoted to medicine.

myth.tradition: Imhotep was history's first great physician, the true 'father of medicine', and perhaps the author of the Edwin Smith surgical papyrus.
myth.record: Sources from his lifetime show an architect-official and priest. Nothing ties him to medicine for some two thousand years; the healer-god belongs to the Late Period and Greco-Roman Egypt.

links.note: Greeks identified the deified Imhotep with Asclepius.

title: The earliest healers known by name

confidence.note: Hesy-Ra, Iry and Peseshet are known from Old Kingdom inscriptions, but their exact reigns are not fixed in the sources used here, and it is debated whether Hesy-Ra was a practicing doctor. That Merit Ptah is a 1930s construction with no ancient evidence behind her is the conclusion of a peer-reviewed study.

people: Hesy-Ra (c. 2650 BCE), 'chief of dentists and doctors' under Djoser

summary: Egypt's tombs name some of the earliest known doctors, from a royal 'guardian of the anus' to Peseshet, overseer of healer women. Merit Ptah, the 'first woman doctor', never existed.
body: The earliest healer known by name may be Hesy-Ra, 'chief of dentists and doctors' under King Djoser, though whether he practiced medicine or supervised healing at court is debated. Better documented is Iry, a court physician whose tombstone was found at Giza: head of the palace doctors, 'palace eye-physician' and 'palace physician of the belly', with the title 'guardian of the anus'. A woman, Peseshet, is named in her son's tomb as 'overseer of healer women'.
Merit Ptah, widely hailed as the first woman physician, is not real: Jakub Kwiecinski traced her to a 1930s misreading by the historian Kate Campbell Hurd-Mead.

myth.tradition: Merit Ptah, an Old Kingdom court physician, was the first woman doctor known to history.
myth.record: No woman physician of that name appears in the ancient record: the name occurs only as a tomb owner's wife in the New Kingdom. Kwiecinski argues the story began in the 1930s when Hurd-Mead garbled a report of Peseshet, a genuine 'overseer of healer women'.

links.note: The famous name with no medical title, beside the obscure ones that have them.
The surviving copy was made centuries after these specialists practiced.

title: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus

confidence.note: Modern reviews date the papyrus to about 1825–1835 BCE (Middle Kingdom), while Breasted in 1930 thought the fragments perhaps as old as 2000 BCE, so the range is wide. Their content is clear, but how much older the treatise itself is cannot be known.

people: F. Ll. Griffith, Egyptologist who published the papyri in 1898
summary: Scraps of a treatise on women's diseases from Kahun are among the oldest medical papyri, older than the famous Ebers and Edwin Smith rolls.
body: Scanty remains of a treatise on diseases of women, found at Kahun (Lahun) and published by F. Ll. Griffith in 1898, are among the oldest surviving medical papyri. Modern reviews date the copy to about 1825–1835 BCE, in the Middle Kingdom; Breasted thought the fragments perhaps as old as 2000 BCE. Its 34 sections cover gynecology, conception and contraception, with non-surgical remedies such as fumigation, massage and pessaries. Breasted noted that, unlike the later Ebers Papyrus, it is a specialist work, and that, like the Edwin Smith Papyrus, it frames its cases with 'instructions'.

title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus

confidence.note: The papyrus is dated by its handwriting to the 17th century BCE. Its archaic language suggests it copies an older text, which is widely accepted, but how much older, and who wrote the original, are unknown.

people: Edwin Smith (1822–1906), American collector who bought it at Luxor in 1862
James Henry Breasted, Egyptologist who published the translation in 1930
summary: An Egyptian scribe copying an old book on wounds stopped mid-sentence c. 1600 BCE. What survives is the oldest known surgical treatise, with 48 cases from head to spine.
body: Sometime around 1600 BCE, a scribe in Egypt sat copying an old book on wounds. He worked down the body from the top of the head, through the face, neck, arms and chest, case after case, and then, partway through case 48, an injury of the spine, he stopped in the middle of a sentence. The result is the Edwin Smith Papyrus, the oldest known surgical treatise.

Cases follow a nearly fixed order: a title, an examination, a diagnosis ending in one of three verdicts (an ailment the practitioner will treat, one he will contend with, or one not to be treated), then treatment where there is any. That last verdict, which James Henry Breasted found in no other Egyptian medical text, appears 14 times, once by an evident scribal slip: the author described injuries he knew he could not cure, because they were worth describing. Magic appears in only one of the 48 cases. The text contains what Breasted announced as the earliest known word for 'brain', and likens the brain's surface to the corrugations on metal slag.

The book was already old when copied. Its terms had grown so obscure that an ancient editor added 69 explanatory glosses; one explains that to 'moor him at his mooring stakes' means to put the patient on his usual diet. Breasted placed the original in the Pyramid Age, at least a thousand years before the copy. A recent reappraisal summarized that the surviving copy was most likely penned in the 17th century BCE and probably reproduces an older document; the original's date and author remain unknown.

Edwin Smith, an American living at Thebes, bought the roll in 1862; after his death in 1906 his daughter gave it to the New-York Historical Society, and Breasted published his translation in 1930. Its back holds a different world: incantations against pestilence and a recipe for turning an old man young, added later. Breasted's suggestion that Imhotep wrote the original, which he himself called pure conjecture, is still repeated, though nothing links Imhotep to medicine until some two thousand years after his death.

myth.tradition: The papyrus was written by Imhotep and shows Egyptian surgery free of magic.
myth.record: The author is unknown; Breasted offered Imhotep as 'pure conjecture'. The treatise itself is strikingly practical, but the same roll carries incantations and a rejuvenation recipe on its back.

links.note: A passage on the heart appears in both papyri.
An earlier specialist treatise in the same case format.

title: The Ebers Papyrus

confidence.note: Breasted dates the manuscript to the early 16th century BCE, and a calendar on its back has been used since the 1860s to date it to about the mid-16th century; Osler gave about 1500 BCE. Its contents are not in doubt, but the original treatises it compiles are older and undated.

place: Thebes (modern Luxor), Egypt; now at Leipzig
people: Georg Ebers (1837–1898), Egyptologist and novelist who bought and published it
Edwin Smith (1822–1906), collector who sold it
summary: Egypt's biggest surviving medical book, a 20-meter roll of prescriptions, charms and a few careful diagnoses, compiled from older treatises c. 1550 BCE.
body: The Ebers Papyrus is the largest medical book to survive from ancient Egypt: a roll of 110 columns, more than 20 meters long, copied in the early 16th century BCE. It is less one book than a library, stitched together from many specialist treatises. Most of it is prescriptions for named complaints, 877 by James Henry Breasted's count, mixed with incantations and charms.

Only near the end does it record how a patient was examined and diagnosed, 47 times in all. One passage on the heart, introduced as from a 'Secret Book of the Physician', also appears in the Edwin Smith Papyrus; Breasted thought the Ebers scribe was quoting the treatise preserved there.

Its modern story is a tangle. Georg Ebers told of a roll found between the legs of a mummy at Thebes, a tale that has been called a romance. In fact he bought it in 1872 from the American collector Edwin Smith and published it at Leipzig in 1875; it is now in the Leipzig library.

title: The Cairo toe

confidence.note: The University of Manchester release dates the toes only as older than 600 BCE, so the age is known only roughly, and the earlier bound of the range is a judgment, not a sourced figure. That the toe worked rests on replica tests with two volunteers plus its design, which Finch argues suggest use in life rather than a burial fitting.

place: Egypt; now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo
people: Jacky Finch, University of Manchester Egyptologist who tested replicas
summary: A wood-and-leather big toe found on an Egyptian mummy let modern volunteers walk comfortably in sandals, making it a strong candidate for the oldest working prosthesis.
body: A three-part artificial big toe of wood and leather, found attached to the foot of an Egyptian mummy and now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, may be among the earliest functional prosthetic body parts. In 2011 Jacky Finch of the University of Manchester had two volunteers who had lost their right big toe walk on exact replicas of it, and of a cartonnage toe in the British Museum, wearing replica Egyptian sandals. One volunteer walked extremely well with both, and both found the Cairo toe particularly comfortable. Its hinge and flattened underside led Finch to suggest it was worn in life.

links.note: Another window on practical Egyptian care for injuries.
